_comment: Shahnama of Firdausi, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905-1925), vols. VI-VIII: Sasanian cycle — Bahram Gur, Nushirwan's chess, Khusrau Parwiz. Paraphrase passages with notes.

title.en: Bahram Gur Cancels a Hundredfold of Taxes
title.zh: 巴赫拉姆·古爾免征積欠

region.zh: 帕爾斯伊斯塔赫爾（象徵性定位）

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. VII, Bahram Gur secs. 1-2

summary.en: Whenas Bahram Gur sat upon the throne the sun acclaimed him while the Shah adored the Maker. I give Him thanks for all His benefits; do ye too praise Him, and strive to keep His covenant unbroken. He bade Gushasp the scribe and Jawanwi the chief accountant approach, ordered them to cancel all arrears of taxes for the Iranians, and they added up the sum of the arrears and found it ninety and a hundred times three hundred thousand drachms: these he forgave, and burnt the registers, and all men rejoiced thereat, flung musk upon the Fire and blessed Bahram where New Year's Day and Sada feast were kept.
summary.zh: 巴赫拉姆·古爾登基，向造物主頌恩：「當讚美祂，謹守祂的盟約。」他命書記與稅務總管清點伊朗積欠的賦稅，共計九萬又三十萬德拉克馬——盡數豁免、焚燬稅冊；萬民歡騰，在歲首與薩達節之所向聖火撒香、祝福君王。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; Bahram V (Bahram Gur), r. 420-438 CE. No living community restriction.

passages.text: Whenas Bahram Gur sat upon the throne the sun acclaimed him while the Shah adored the Maker, the all-seeing, watchful World-lord, the Lord of victory and majesty, the Lord of increase and of loss, then said: for He hath fashioned fortune, and my hopes and fears are all in Him. I give Him thanks for all His benefits; do ye too praise Him, and strive to keep His covenant unbroken.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Bahram Gur sec. 1 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Shah, that man of lore, then bade Gushasp, the scribe, with prudent Jawanwi, the chief accountant, approach, and ordered them to cancel all arrears of taxes for the Iranians. These two wise scribes went to their registers, added up the sum of the arrears, and found it ninety and a hundred times three hundred thousand drachms. These he forgave, and burnt the registers, and all men rejoiced thereat. Where New Year's Day and Sada feast were kept they flung musk upon the Fire and blessed Bahram the Shah.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Bahram Gur sec. 2 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Bahram Gur Guest of the Water-carrier and the Jew

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. VII, Bahram Gur secs. 3-5

summary.en: In disguise the Shah goes to the house of Lambak the water-carrier, who pledges his water-skins to buy a feast, and the king cuts up the meat himself and cooks it: we have been jolly in this house three days. Next night he knocks at the door of barren Baraham the Jew, who treats him scurvily — the Jew is very poor and every night reposeth, bare and hungry, on the ground — and Bahram, lodging outside, learns how the miser hoards; next day he seizes Baraham's hoards and bestows them all upon Lambak the poor host.
summary.zh: 君王微服投宿汲水人蘭巴克家中；窮漢典當水囊備宴，王親自切肉烹調：「我們在這屋裡快樂了三日！」次夜他敲響吝嗇猶太人巴拉罕的門，遭冷言拒絕——「那猶太人窮得很，夜夜露宿」——王便宿於門外窺其積藏；翌日沒其金庫，盡數賞賜好客的蘭巴克。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source. Bahram's disguise tales feed the Arabian-Nights tradition; read as folklore, not ethnography. No living community restriction.

passages.text: He took to the bazar his water-skins and tackle, which he pledged to some rich man, bought what he needed and returned in haste rejoicing to Bahram. Bahram took the meat promptly from him, cut it up, and then proceeded with the cookery. When they had eaten they took wine and goblet, and first of all drank to the king of kings. Lambak, when they had drunk, prepared for sleep, and set a candle by Bahram Gur's couch.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Bahram Gur sec. 3 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: He stole away and made toward the house of barren Baraham, knocked at the door, and said: the Shah hath come back from the chase, but I was left behind; 'tis night and I know not the way; if I may sojourn in this house to-night I will not trouble any one. The messenger departed and said: there is no shelter here for thee. The Jew is very poor and every night reposeth, bare and hungry, on the ground.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Bahram Gur sec. 4 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Bahram replied: I will not enter but will sleep outside, and in the morning he saw how Baraham kept his hoards; he seized the wealth of Baraham, and bestowed it all upon Lambak the water-carrier who had feasted him, so that the generous host was recompensed a hundredfold and the churl went empty away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Bahram Gur sec. 5 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Bahram Gur Brings the Lute-folk from Hind
title.zh: 巴赫拉姆自印度引入樂師

region.en: Roads of Hind and Iran (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 印度至伊朗之路（象徵性定位）

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. VII, Bahram Gur sec. 39

summary.en: Bahram sends letters to each archmage asking what folk are free from toil, and the answer comes: the rich wear wreaths of roses in their drinking-bouts and quaff to minstrelsy, but as for us they do not reckon us as men at all. The king of kings laughs heartily and sends a camel-post to king Shangul of Hind: select ten thousand of the Gipsy-tribe, both male and female, skilful on the harp, and send them to me. He accorded them an audience and gave each an ox and ass, for he proposed to make the Gipsies husbandmen; the Gipsies went and ate the wheat and oxen, and came at a year's end with pallid cheeks; and so the Gipsies now have for company the dog and wolf, and tramp unceasingly.
summary.zh: 巴赫拉姆問群臣：「何民不勞而享樂？」答曰：富人花間醉酒、歌舞昇平，而窮人被視如無物。王大笑，遣使印度王香古爾：「選一萬名擅彈豎琴的流浪樂師來！」他們到來後，王賜牛驢、發麥種，欲使其務農兼為窮人奏樂；誰知樂師們吃盡牛麥，一年後灰頭土臉而回。王遂命其「驢背馱琴，四海為家」——從此流浪樂人與犬狼為伴，行蹤不絕。

sensitivity.note: Epic etiology of Romani musicians in Persia (Firdausi via Bahram V); read as medieval legend. No living community restriction.

passages.text: Thereafter he sent letters to each archmage, and asked: in all the realm what folk are free from toil, and who are mendicants and destitute? An answer came from all the archimages, from all the nobles, and the men of lore: the face of earth appeareth prosperous, save that the poor complain against the ills of fortune and the Shah. The rich wear wreaths of roses in their drinking-bouts, and quaff to minstrelsy, but as for us they do not reckon us as men at all. The empty-handed drinketh with no rose or harp. The king of kings should look to it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Bahram Gur sec. 39 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Shah laughed heartily at this report, and sent a camel-post to king Shangul to say thus: O thou monarch good at need! select ten thousand of the Gipsy-tribe, both male and female, skilful on the harp, and send them to me. I may gain mine end through that notorious folk. Now when the letter came to Shangul he made choice of Gipsies as bidden by the Shah who, when they came, accorded them an audience and gave each an ox and ass, for he proposed to make the Gipsies husbandmen.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Bahram Gur sec. 39 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Gipsies went and ate the wheat and oxen, then at a year's end came with pallid cheeks. The Shah said: was it not your task to plough, to sow, and reap? Your asses yet remain, so load them up, prepare your harps, and stretch the silken chords. And so the Gipsies now, according to Bahram's just ordinance, have for company the dog and wolf, and tramp unceasingly.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Bahram Gur sec. 39 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Bahram Gur Dies on the Brocade of His Bed

region.zh: 巴赫拉姆王宮（象徵性定位）

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. VII, Bahram Gur sec. 40

summary.en: Thus passed he three score years and three, and had no equal in that age. The treasury is void, says the archmage, and the monarch answers: take no further pains, for I have passed beyond the need thereof; resign the world to its Creator. He cast away the crown, left his seat, and hasted to resign the world's affairs; at night-fall he was eager for repose, and when the sun displayed its head fear filled the archimage's heart: Yazdagird drew near his sire and spied what froze the breath upon his lips — Bahram with faded cheeks lay dead on gold brocade. Of fifty monarchs of seed royal sown who girt their loins upon the Iranian throne, Bahram Gur had no like in eminence, in justice, puissance, and excellence.
summary.zh: 他在位六十三年，舉世無雙。庫藏已空？他答：「我已無需財貨，把世界交還造物主吧。」他棄冠離座、淡出塵務；夜闌就寢，晨光初露時術士惶恐——王子趨近父王，見其唇齒凝滯：巴赫拉姆面容枯槁，僵臥於金錦之上。王族五十君王之中，論公義、威力與賢明，無出其右者。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source. Firdausi gives Bahram a bed-death; the popular mire-death is a later tradition. No living community restriction.

passages.text: Thus passed he three score years and three, and had no equal in that age. The scribe, the wise archmage, his minister, said to him: the treasury of the king of mighty men is void. The monarch answered: take no further pains, for I have passed beyond the need thereof. Resign the world to its Creator, Him who manifested forth His works. The heavens will pass away, but God abideth ever to guide both thee and me to what is good.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Bahram Gur sec. 40 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Intending to devote himself to God he cast away the crown, he left his seat, and hasted to resign the world's affairs. At night-fall he was eager for repose, and, when the sun displayed its head above the deep, fear filled his archimage's heart, who thought: the Shah ariseth not from sleep unless he hath withdrawn him from the lords. Then Yazdagird drew near his sire and spied what froze the breath upon his lips: Bahram with faded cheeks lay dead on gold brocade!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Bahram Gur sec. 40 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: Of fifty monarchs of seed royal sown, who girt their loins upon the Iranian throne, Bahram Gur had no like in eminence, in justice, puissance, and excellence. Thou wouldst have called king Rustam but vizir to him. Sun, moon, and Venus, Saturn, crown, and throne, a Shah, like this one, ne'er will look upon. He decked the throne and crown, from Rum and Chin took toll and tax, yet passed as he had been a starving mendicant!
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Bahram Gur sec. 40 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

title.en: Buzurjmihr Unravels the Game of Chess

region.zh: 努希爾萬王庭（象徵性定位）

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1905), vol. VII, Nushirwan sec. 1 (Introduction of Chess)

summary.en: The Raja of Hind sends to Nushirwan a chess-board wrought with cunning workmanship: bid the questers for knowledge find out how that goodly game is played, the name of each piece and the way to move it; if they discover it I will send full tribute; but if their knowledge is no match for ours let them pay a tribute unto us, since knowledge is of all famed things the best. The chiefs and archimages examine the board and none discovers how the game is played; then Buzurjmihr comes to the Shah and says: I will discover all this goodly game, employing wisdom as my guide therein — and, retiring, he finds the powers of footman, elephant, rukh, horse, wazir, and king, and wins the wager for Iran.
summary.zh: 印度王公遣使送來一具工巧棋盤：「若伊朗智者能解此局——知各子之名、行法與方格——便奉歲貢；若不能，則爾等當向我納貢，因『知識』乃萬美之首！」群臣術士環棋而思，無人能解；賢相布祖爾吉米赫爾進言：「我憑智慧必解此局！」他退而參悟兵卒、戰象、戰車、駿馬、宰相與王的行法，替伊朗贏下這場以貢賦為注的賭局。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; the Chatrang-namak legend (chess entering Persia under Nushirwan). No living community restriction.

passages.text: The envoy of the king of Hind hath come with elephants, with parasols, with horsemen of Sind and laden camels fifty score. The Raja had amassed from every hand the products of Kannuj and Mai. Then the envoy brought a letter which the Raja had written upon silk to Nushirwan, and also a chess-board wrought with cunning workmanship. The man of Hind thus gave the Raja's message: bid those much travailed in the quest for knowledge to place this board, used in the game of chess, before them and set all their wits to work to find out how that goodly game is played.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Nushirwan sec. 1 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: If they discover all this goodly game, and prove themselves the betters of the wise, then, as the Shah commands, I will send full tribute to his court with all good will; but if the nobles of the Iranian folk have not the wit to resolve the point, since their knowledge is no match for ours, let them not seek for tax and tribute from us, but rather pay a tribute unto us, since knowledge is of all famed things the best. The envoy thus replied: 'tis all, O king! an emblem of the art of war, and thou wilt see the tactics, the plan, and order of a battlefield.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Nushirwan sec. 1 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

passages.text: The chiefs and archimages that were counsellors all came before the Shah and with the chess-board in front of them considered it at large, examined it, tried every device, and played with one another in all ways; but none discovered how the game was played, and all departed louring. Buzurjmihr came to the Shah, perceived him vexed and troubled, and said: O great king, world-lord and vigilant whose word is law! I will discover all this goodly game, employing wisdom as my guide therein.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Nushirwan sec. 1 (Warner 1905); not verbatim.

region.zh: 霍斯勞獵苑（象徵性定位）

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1923), vol. VIII, Khusrau Parwiz sec. 56

summary.en: Khusrau Parwiz like other paladins, while yet his father lived, was young and bold, and had for mate Shirin who was to him as his bright eyes; he cared for none beside among the fair. He parts from her when he comes to be king and has to fight Bahram Chubina, and she weeps day and night o'er his defect in love. When his mighty host rides out, seven hundred falconers, three hundred cheetah-keepers, two thousand minstrels on camel-back, and Shirin, hearing that the host hath come, puts on a yellow vest musk-scented, goes on the roof, and cries in the olden tongue: O Shah! Great Lion! where is that love of thine? Where are our loves, our troth, our bonds, our oaths?
summary.zh: 霍斯勞未登基時英武少年，唯有希琳是他的「明眸」，此外無人入心。即位後為戰巴赫拉姆·丘賓而別離，她晝夜泣血。皇家獵隊出行——七百鷹師、三百馴豹人、兩千駝背樂師——希琳聞王駕至，披灑著麝香的鵝黃羅衫登樓遠眺，以古語泣呼：「大王啊，雄獅！你的愛在哪裡？我們的山盟海誓、我們的癡情，都到哪裡去了？」

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; the Shahnama's version of Khusrau and Shirin (cf. Nizami's romance). No living community restriction.

passages.text: Khusrau Parwiz like other paladins, while yet his father lived, was young and bold, and had for mate Shirin who was to him as his bright eyes. He cared for none beside among the fair, but parted from her for a while when he came to be king and had to roam the world unrestingly, for all his work was then to fight Bahram Chubina, while the Fair wept day and night o'er his defect in love.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Khusrau Parwiz sec. 56 (Warner 1923); not verbatim.

passages.text: It was so that one day he willed to hunt, and all things were prepared as in the times of former Shahs: three hundred steeds caparisoned with gold, a thousand and eight score afoot, seven hundred falconers with royal falcons, three hundred keepers of the cheetahs, and two thousand minstrels all on camel-back, crowned with gold.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Khusrau Parwiz sec. 56 (Warner 1923); not verbatim.

passages.text: Now Shirin, on hearing that the host, preceded by the mighty Shah, hath come, put on a yellow vest musk-scented, and made her visage like pomegranate-blooms; she left her jocund hall, went on the roof, and waited till Khusrau Parwiz arrived, then let the tear-drops fall upon her cheeks. All tears and beauty, eagerly she cried thus in the olden tongue: O Shah! Great Lion! where is that love of thine? Where are the tears of blood once stanched by looking on Shirin? Where are our loves, our troth, our bonds, our oaths?
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Khusrau Parwiz sec. 56 (Warner 1923); not verbatim.

title.en: Barbad Sings Hidden in the Plane-Tree

region.zh: 霍斯勞御苑（象徵性定位）

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1923), vol. VIII, Khusrau Parwiz sec. 60

summary.en: When none fared ill at court Barbad heard tell of the minstrel Mardwi, the rival harper of the Shah, and dressed all in green and took his harp, and, when the Shah came to the pleasance, climbed into a plane-tree and sang while the monarch quaffed. None but Barbad can play so, thought the Shah; then while Barbad sang on the monarch filled the singer's mouth with jewels, and Barbad became the first of harpers. The epoch of Barbad hath past and gone: that market never failed while he could strike the strings.
summary.zh: 宮中太平無事，樂師巴爾巴德聞御前樂正馬爾德維之名，遂綠衣抱琴入御苑，攀上懸鈴木，當王獨酌時在高枝上放歌。王驚：「除巴爾巴德誰能彈得如此！」邊聽歌邊將寶石填滿歌者之口——巴爾巴德自此成為首席樂師。「巴爾巴德的時代已成過往：只要琴弦還在，那市集永不冷落。」

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; Barbad is the famed Sasanian court musician. No living community restriction.

passages.text: When none fared ill at court, Barbad heard tell of the minstrel Mardwi, and Barbad approached Mardwi forthwith; the Shah is coming to the pleasance, said Barbad, and dressed all in green and took his harp. And thought the Shah: none but Barbad can play so. Then while Barbad sang on the monarch quaffed. He filled the singer's mouth. Barbad became the first of harpers. The epoch of Barbad hath past and gone: that market never failed while he could strike the strings.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Khusrau Parwiz sec. 60 (Warner 1923); not verbatim.

title.en: Khusrau Parwiz Deposed and Sent to Taisafun
title.zh: 霍斯勞失位被囚泰西封

source.work: Firdausi, Shahnama, trans. A. G. & E. Warner (1923), vol. VIII, Khusrau Parwiz sec. 65

summary.en: The Shah bode in that mead, a lofty tree overshadowing him, and when he hungered he bade his slave cut off a cantle from that costly belt, five studs of gold enriched with jewelry, and send the gardener to the bazar for bread. The jeweller cries: who will dare to buy, for this should be within the treasury of Khusrau Parwiz? Shirwi knows: 'tis Khusrau Parwiz, and sends three hundred horsemen; the astrologers had said to the king: thy death will come to thee between two heights, and by a slave's hand in a lonely spot. He mounts the elephant, crying in the ancient tongue: O treasure! if thou art my foe be not a friend to these mine enemies, for I am in the hands of Ahriman to-day — and Kubad gives orders: let trusty Galimis be made his keeper at Taisafun with a thousand horsemen.
summary.zh: 失位的霍斯勞匿身河畔樹蔭下，飢時命僕割下腰帶上五枚寶石換麵包；珠寶商驚呼：「這是霍斯勞王庫中之物！」其子希爾維遂遣三百騎尋獲。星占家曾言：他將死於「兩座高牆之間、荒僻處、奴僕之手」。他騎上大象，以古語哀呼：「寶藏啊，若你與我為敵，也莫要助我的仇人——今日我落入阿赫里曼之手！」希爾維登基，命忠僕加里米斯率千騎將他押往泰西封看管。

sensitivity.note: Epic literary source; the deposition of Khusrau II (628 CE) as Firdausi tells it. No living community restriction.

passages.text: The Shah bode in that mead, a lofty tree overshadowing him. When half the longsome day had passed he hungered. Now within the pleasance there was a man employed who did not know the king by sight. The Sun-faced bade his slave: cut off a cantle from this costly belt. That cantle had on it five studs of gold enriched with jewelry, and the king then spake thus to the gardener: these studs will prove of use to-day; go thou to the bazar, buy meat and bread, and shun frequented paths.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Khusrau Parwiz sec. 65 (Warner 1923); not verbatim.

passages.text: The expert, when he looked upon the studs, said: who will dare to buy, for this should be within the treasury of Khusrau Parwiz, who hath a hundred new like this each year? Whom didst thou steal these jewels from? Shirwi knew: 'tis Khusrau Parwiz, his features are the age's cynosure, and sent three hundred horsemen from the court. Meanwhile his heart was troubled at his aged fortune because astrologers had said to him: thy death will come to thee between two heights, and by a slave's hand in a lonely spot.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Khusrau Parwiz sec. 65 (Warner 1923); not verbatim.

passages.text: So now this armour is mine earth, my golden shield my heaven, and the heights are my two treasuries within the garden. In sooth my days are coming to an end: where is my star that used to light the world? They brought an elephant for him. His soul was dark with woe. He mounted, and the troops led him away while in the ancient tongue he cried: O treasure! if thou art my foe be not a friend to these mine enemies, for I am in the hands of Ahriman to-day. Kubad gave orders to his minister: bid them carry him to Taisafun away from court with his own counsellor; there let him bide in peace for many a day and harmed by none.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Firdausi, Shahnama, Khusrau Parwiz sec. 65 (Warner 1923); not verbatim.
